name: Americanism (ideology)
summary: Americanism is loyalty to the United States and to the political creed its defining sources see as its founding principles. In its best-known form, the 'one hundred percent Americanism' of Theodore Roosevelt and the Americanization movement, it demands undivided national allegiance, the English language and the assimilation of immigrants, judges citizens by conduct rather than ancestry or creed, and keeps church and state apart. A second strand, set out by C. Bradley Thompson with Ayn Rand's and Leonard Read's texts, reads it as the individual-rights philosophy of the Declaration of Independence: limited government, private property and free exchange. The word is famously contested, and its sources divide wherever these strands, or the later left and right uses Thompson reports, disagree.
scope: As the defining sources set it out: the Encyclopedia of European Social History entry (s7) treats Americanism as the American equivalent of nationalism, the post-1918 'one hundred percent Americanism' movement, and in another sense the central tenets of the American creed; Olneck (s8) describes the creedal American identity and the World War I campaigns for 100 Percent Americanism; Dorsey (s9) ties Roosevelt's speeches and essays to his Americanism; Thompson (s6) defines it as the Declaration's individual-rights philosophy, names Rand's Textbook of Americanism and Read's 'The Essence of Americanism' as its classic statements, and reports that the Left now identifies it with multiculturalism, regulation and welfarism and the Right with Christianity, school prayer, tradition, family values and community standards. The profile answers from these sources and the texts they tie to the term: Roosevelt's 'True Americanism' (1894) and 'Americanism' (1915), the American Legion's preamble ('one hundred percent Americanism') and its magazine's account of that Americanism, Rand's Textbook and Read's speech. Where these strands, or the uses Thompson documents, take opposite sides it is a split (0, low). Catholic 'Americanism' (the heresy condemned in 1899), nativist and Klan claims to the word, and the Communist Party's slogan are outside the profile, as are the broader subjects American nationalism, exceptionalism and civil religion. Kazin and McCartin's Americanism (2006), Gelernter's Americanism (2007) and Wall's Inventing the 'American Way' could not be read in an open copy.

sources.title: Americanism (ideology)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: First pass only (kept for the reviewHistory). Under rules 5 Wikipedia is not evidence; this pass used it only for leads (Thompson, Kazin and McCartin, Roosevelt, Rand).

sources.title: Americanism (address to the Knights of Columbus, Carnegie Hall, 12 October 1915)
sources.author: Theodore Roosevelt (Project Gutenberg #68152)
sources.usedFor: Read in full: equal treatment regardless of ancestry or creed, separation of church and state, no hyphenated Americans, undivided allegiance, English as the common language, deportation of aliens who refuse it, duty before rights, employer-worker partnership, universal military service and a larger army and navy. Dorsey (s9) presents Roosevelt's speeches and essays as the statement of his Americanism.

sources.title: Preamble to the Constitution of The American Legion
sources.author: The American Legion
sources.usedFor: 'To foster and perpetuate a one hundred percent Americanism', the movement the Encyclopedia of European Social History (s7) and Olneck (s8) name: Constitution, law and order, individual obligation, combating the autocracy of classes and masses, justice, freedom and democracy.

sources.title: The Gettysburg Address
sources.author: Abraham Lincoln
sources.usedFor: First pass only (kept for the reviewHistory). None of the defining sources of this pass ties the address to Americanism, so it is not used for current answers.

sources.title: American exceptionalism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: First pass only (kept for the reviewHistory); a related subject's article, not evidence.

sources.title: Defining Americanism
sources.author: C. Bradley Thompson (Clemson University), Cato Unbound, 23 March 2011
sources.usedFor: Definition of Americanism as the individual-rights philosophy of the Declaration (separation of church, school, economy and culture from the state; free production and exchange; keeping one's wealth); its contested meaning, with the Left identifying it with multiculturalism, regulation and welfarism and the Right with Christianity, school prayer, tradition, family values and community standards; names Rand's Textbook of Americanism and Read's 'The Essence of Americanism' as classic statements. Read in full.

sources.title: America, Americanization, and Anti-Americanism
sources.author: Encyclopedia of European Social History (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com
sources.usedFor: Definition: in the United States Americanism is the American equivalent of nationalism, after World War I the 'one hundred percent Americanism' movement confronting immigrants with criteria for inclusion, and in another sense the central tenets of the American creed.

sources.title: Americanization, U.S.
sources.author: Michael R. Olneck, New Dictionary of the History of Ideas (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com
sources.usedFor: The creedal American identity and the World War I campaigns against hyphenation and for '100 Percent Americanism': total national loyalty, naturalization, quick acquisition and sole use of English, conformity to American norms.

sources.title: We Are All Americans, Pure and Simple: Theodore Roosevelt and the Myth of Americanism (book page and publisher's description)
sources.author: Leroy G. Dorsey (University of Alabama Press), via UBC Press
sources.usedFor: Ties Roosevelt's speeches and essays to Americanism: everyone could become 'Americans, pure and simple' by embracing his Americanism, a rhetorical melting pot.

sources.title: True Americanism (The Forum, April 1894)
sources.author: Theodore Roosevelt (excerpts, Teaching American History)
sources.usedFor: Americanism as spirit, not creed or birthplace; national rather than sectional; Americanizing immigrants in speech, political ideas and church-state relations; English-only public schools; no division of the school fund; no ethnic or religious voting; drastic immigration restriction including races that do not assimilate readily.

sources.title: Textbook of Americanism (The Vigil, 1946)
sources.author: Ayn Rand (FEE's PDF of the copy Rand delivered to Leonard Read)
sources.usedFor: Named by Thompson (s6) as a classic statement of Americanism. Read in full (twelve sections, OCR): individualism against collectivism, unalienable individual rights, limited power of society, no initiation of force, government limited to retaliatory force, no mixed system, objective moral code.

sources.title: The Essence of Americanism (1961)
sources.author: Leonard E. Read, Foundation for Economic Education
sources.usedFor: Named by Thompson (s6) as a statement of Americanism. Read in full: the Declaration's rights from the Creator, the Constitution and Bill of Rights as limits on government, private property, self-reliance, against the welfare state, Social Security, farm subsidies, public housing, inflation and socialism; free exchange.

sources.title: The definition of Americanism
sources.author: Jeff Stoffer, The American Legion Magazine, 22 January 2019
sources.usedFor: The Legion's account of the Americanism it was founded to foster (s3): opposition to communism, fascism and Nazism, its 1923 resolution against racial, religious and class strife, citizenship and flag education in schools, the 1963 and current definitions.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Roosevelt's Americanism address calls for a greatly enlarged army and navy and universal military service.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Read praises America's high degree of specialisation and says everyone depends on the free exchange of specialties.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Rand's Textbook defends the wage job as a voluntary contract a worker may quit, unlike slavery, and Read calls money the indispensable circulatory system of a specialised economy.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Rand's Textbook says the government's duty is to arrest criminals and protect individuals against criminal attack.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: Rand's Textbook treats wage employment as a voluntary contract between free men, not a form of slavery.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: Read traces America's growth to the private property principle that replaced the Pilgrims' common holding.

allow-dual-citizenship.rationale: Roosevelt demands a citizenship absolutely undivided that repudiates all duality of national loyalty, and immigrants who have renounced allegiance to every foreign government.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Roosevelt calls it wicked to support or oppose a man because of his creed and extends that to the man all creeds would call unorthodox.

arms-reduction.rationale: Roosevelt wants the army and navy greatly increased, with more ships, artillery and ammunition.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Roosevelt and the Americanization movement demanded that immigrants give up Old-World speech and customs, but Thompson documents that the Left now identifies Americanism with multiculturalism; the uses of the word divide.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Read says governments that run deficits finance them by inflation, which he calls the most unjust and cruel tax of all.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Read says the private property principle started an era of growth that led to the American miracle of production and self-reliance.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Thompson defines Americanism as separating culture from the state but documents a right-wing Americanism of community standards; the uses of the word divide.

central-planning.rationale: Read names the belief in using government force to control citizens' productive and creative activity as the common disease of socialism, communism, fascism and the New Deal.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Read says people should turn to themselves rather than to government for welfare, while Thompson reports that the Left identifies Americanism with welfarism; the uses of the word divide.

class-collaboration.rationale: Roosevelt's 1915 address wants the relation between employer and worker to be one of partnership and comradeship, and condemns drawing political lines between class and class.

collective-farming.rationale: Read says the Pilgrims' common warehouse left them starving and dying, and that Bradford's turn to each family working for its own merit ended the famine.

communal-electorates.rationale: Roosevelt's 1894 essay says there is no room for a German-American or Irish-American vote and that all citizens should vote solely as Americans.

conscription.rationale: Roosevelt calls universal military service on the Swiss model the most important of all things for national defence, and the Legion's founders scorned the immigrant 'alien slackers' who avoided the draft.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Thompson defines Americanism as self-government in the fullest sense, and Roosevelt calls the nation's principles those of free popular government.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Read's account of the Pilgrims has the colony's common property and common warehouse end in starvation until private property replaced it.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Rand's Textbook says a million men cannot pass a law to kill one man, and that the Constitution limits the power of society over the individual.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Read counts the welfare state as socialism and praises a time when no one turned to government for welfare, while Thompson reports that the Left identifies Americanism with welfarism; the uses of the word divide.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Roosevelt says that in war each labour organisation must be subordinated to the service of the nation, and calls those who use the foreign vote engaged in treason.

democracy-best.rationale: Roosevelt calls the nation's founding principles the system of free popular government and America a great democratic experiment, and the Legion pledges to pass on the principles of democracy; neither speaks of bad choices by voters.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The Legion preamble pledges to combat the autocracy of both the classes and the masses.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Read's speech opens with the Pilgrim colony starving under 'from each according to ability, to each according to need' until it adopted distribution by merit.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Read says the Creator, not the state, endows man's rights, but calls officials the people's agents holding force the people delegated to them.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Roosevelt calls for the patriotism that puts devotion to duty before individual rights, while Rand's Textbook holds that rights are unalienable and that no man exists for the sake of the group; the texts divide.

economic-freedom.rationale: Rand's Textbook says that without private property no independent action is possible, and Read calls Americanism at once a spiritual, political and economic concept.

elective-rulers.rationale: Roosevelt praises free popular government and wants immigrants to honour Washington's birthday instead of the Queen's or the Kaiser's, and the Legion stands for democracy.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Read calls the Constitution and Bill of Rights a set of prohibitions against over-extended government, and Rand's Textbook says society may make only laws that do not violate individual rights.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Roosevelt's 1915 address says each man is to be treated on his worth without regard to ancestry or creed, and Rand's Textbook holds that men are equal before the law at all times.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Read tells how the Pilgrims starved under 'to each according to need' until Bradford introduced 'to each according to merit', the principle he says built America.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Roosevelt calls America the experiment of making a new nation out of divers race stocks and says Americanism is a question of spirit, not of creed or birthplace.

family-wage.rationale: Roosevelt says America cannot afford low wage rates that sacrifice individual and family life and must maintain the American standard of living.

farm-price-support.rationale: Read likens the repeal of Britain's Corn Laws, which he praises, to repealing subsidies to American farmers.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Roosevelt says there should be no denial or limitation of the alien's opportunity to work and to own property.

free-trade.rationale: Read holds up Cobden, Bright and Bastiat's freedom of exchange and the repeal of the Corn Laws as the reform that brought Britain unparalleled prosperity.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Rand's Textbook says that if you must obtain society's permission before acting you are not free, whether the permission is granted or not.

harm-principle.rationale: Rand's Textbook allows force only against those who initiate it, but Thompson reports a right-wing Americanism of community standards and family values; the uses of the word divide.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Roosevelt says no man can be a good citizen unless learning the language and that aliens who do not learn English within a set time should be deported; the Americanization movement made English its first demand.

immigration-favours-shared-culture.rationale: Roosevelt's 1894 essay wants immigration laws that keep out those who do not assimilate readily.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Read welcomes the repeal of Britain's Poor Laws as equivalent to repealing Social Security, but Thompson reports that the Left identifies Americanism with welfarism; the uses of the word divide.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Rand's Textbook says rights belong to each man as an individual, not to men as a group or collective.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Read celebrates the American miracle of production and the most advanced division-of-labor society that has ever existed.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Roosevelt calls any union of church and state contrary to the spirit of the Constitution, and Thompson lists the separation of church and state among Americanism's principles.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Read's 'Essence of Americanism' credits private enterprise with building more housing per person than any other country and calls government control of productive activity the disease behind socialism; Roosevelt's addresses do not take up the question.

military-superiority.rationale: Roosevelt asks for battleships, battle cruisers, submarines, artillery and a far larger and more efficient army and navy so the nation can hold its own against aggression; he does not speak of superiority.

minority-language-support.rationale: Roosevelt wants all school exercises in English and no other language, and aliens who do not learn English within a set time deported.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Roosevelt warns that a tangle of nationalities each preserving its separate nationality would bring the nation to ruin.

more-religion-public.rationale: Roosevelt demands complete severance of church and state and Thompson the separation of church and state, while Thompson reports that the Right identifies Americanism with Christianity and school prayer; the uses of the word divide.

nation-first.rationale: Roosevelt wants officials who weigh nothing beyond the honour and interest of the United States save the general welfare of humanity, and his 1894 essay quotes with approval 'America, first, last, and all the time'.

national-church-status.rationale: Roosevelt opposes any recognition by the state in any shape or form of a creed's schools and says no creed should be aided by the state.

native-born-offices.rationale: Roosevelt says a naturalized citizen who has become an American stands on exactly the same footing as any native-born citizen, and that opposing a man for his birthplace is a base outrage.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Rand's Textbook says there can be no social system mixing individualism and collectivism and that a supposedly mixed society is merely disintegrating.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Rand's Textbook says the law must let a man protect himself and likens just government to a man who kills in self-defence.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Rand and Thompson limit government to protecting individual rights, while Roosevelt calls the policy of 'let alone' thoroughly vicious and wants government training, planning and care for immigrants' welfare; the texts divide.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Roosevelt calls it a cardinal sin against democracy to support or oppose a man for office because of his creed, and political movements along sectarian lines an assault on Americanism.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Roosevelt wants non-sectarian public schools with no public money for sectarian purposes, but Thompson reports a right-wing Americanism of school prayer; the uses of the word divide.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Roosevelt says an employer who does not treat his workers as partners and care for their welfare is recreant to his duty as an American citizen.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Legion presents its Americanism as early and firm opposition to anti-democratic ideologies, communism, fascism and Nazism, and its preamble pledges to safeguard the principles of justice, freedom and democracy.

open-borders.rationale: Roosevelt says an immigrant not fit to become a citizen should not be allowed to come, and calls in 1894 for drastic laws to regulate immigration.

patriotic-education.rationale: The Legion's Americanism programme teaches flag respect, citizenship and the Constitution to schoolchildren, and Roosevelt wants every citizen trained by every means to realise his duty to the nation.

people-in-arms.rationale: Roosevelt pairs universal service with a much larger regular army and navy and a regular reserve rather than replacing them.

person-over-state.rationale: Rand's Textbook holds that each man exists by his own right and for his own sake, not for the sake of the group.

population-transfer.rationale: Roosevelt says the hyphenated American whose heart-allegiance lies abroad has no place here and should return, and that aliens who refuse to learn English within a set time should be deported.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Roosevelt's 1894 essay wants Americans to keep their civilization distinctively their own rather than imitate Europe, but Thompson says folkways do not capture Americanism and rejects the Right's identification of it with tradition; the sources divide.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Read cites post-Napoleonic Britain's controls on production and prices as a case where people would have starved but for the smugglers.

price-controls-fight-inflation.rationale: Read blames inflation on government fiscal policy and points to Britain's controls on production and prices as a cause of near-starvation.

price-stability-first.rationale: Read calls inflation the most unjust and cruel tax of all and warns that it can wreck the exchange on which a specialised economy depends.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Rand's Textbook says men delegate to the government the power to use force in retaliation, so courts and policing belong to the state.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Rand's Textbook warns against thinking of a worker as a slave: he holds his job by a voluntary contract he can leave.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Rand's Textbook says rights mark an objective division not subject to the arbitrary decree of society, and that men need a defined code to know what to expect.

property-fundamental.rationale: Rand's Textbook names individual property as part of the unalienable right of liberty, without which no independent action is possible, and Read calls the right to the fruits of one's labour the private property principle on which America grew.

property-sabotage-justified.rationale: Roosevelt's 1915 address condemns the incitement of strikes and sabotage that destroy property in American plants.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Rand's Textbook calls 'the public good comes above any individual rights' an empty, vicious collectivist slogan and treats property as an unalienable individual right.

public-ownership.rationale: Read defines socialism as state ownership and control of the means of production and asks Americanists to refuse any hand in supporting socialistic activity.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Roosevelt's 1915 address treats the right to hold and express any religious view, the unorthodox included, as a core American principle and rejects any union of church and state.

race-based-immigration-restrictions.rationale: Roosevelt's 1894 essay wants drastic laws to keep out races which do not assimilate readily with our own.

racial-franchise.rationale: Roosevelt wants every citizen judged on his conduct alone and race prejudice eliminated, and Thompson counts the freeing of the slaves and the end of oppressive laws as Americanism's work.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Roosevelt calls voting as a German-American or Irish-American treason to American institutions, and the Legion's 1923 resolution brands fostering racial strife un-American.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Thompson names the institutionalised discrimination against African-Americans after emancipation as a failure to live up to Americanism, and Roosevelt calls for the elimination of race prejudice.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Roosevelt's 1894 essay calls it urgently necessary to check and regulate immigration by much more drastic laws; in 1915 he would bar any immigrant unfit to become a citizen though he opposed a literacy test.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Thompson defines Americanism as separating economy and state but documents that the Left identifies it with regulation, and Roosevelt's 1915 address calls a corporation that ignores its duties anti-social; the uses of the word divide on this.

religion-illusion.rationale: Read grounds Americanism in the Creator as the endower of man's rights and calls its loss the forgetting of America's spiritual antecedent.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Roosevelt says union of church and state is partly accomplished wherever a given creed is aided by the state, and wants no discrimination for or against any.

religious-nation.rationale: Roosevelt says Americanism is a question of spirit, not of creed, but Thompson reports that the Right identifies Americanism with Christianity; the uses of the word divide.

remove-other-ethnic-groups-from-country.rationale: Roosevelt's 1915 address wants Americans of every ancestry to stand together for the elimination of race prejudice in one united nation.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Thompson treats the Declaration of Independence, the founding act of resistance to the British crown, as Americanism's heroic founding action.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Roosevelt names the right to hold and express the religious views that meet one's own soul's needs as one of the most important things to secure.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Roosevelt condemns foreign governments funding centres, societies and a foreign-language press to keep immigrants loyal to them and wants Americans to do this work themselves.

restrict-private-adult-pornography-acces.rationale: Thompson's Americanism separates culture and state, while the right-wing Americanism he reports stands for community standards; the uses of the word divide.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Rand's Textbook calls the notion that expediency is the practical guide to action childish and says no society can exist without a moral principle.

right-to-secede.rationale: Roosevelt's 1894 essay says American nationality has been settled once for all and contrasts it with the provincial spirit that broke Spanish America into squabbling states.

school-vouchers.rationale: Roosevelt's 1894 essay stands for the public-school system in its entirety and against any division of the school fund or state aid to parochial schools.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Rand's Textbook says each man exists for his own sake and may pursue his own happiness, while Roosevelt's 1915 address asks citizens to put devotion to duty before their individual rights; the texts divide.

self-ownership.rationale: Rand's Textbook defines collectivism as holding that a man's work, body and personality belong to the group, and Americanism as its opposite.

separate-church-state.rationale: Roosevelt holds there must be complete severance of church and state and Thompson lists the separation of church and state, but Thompson documents a right-wing Americanism of Christianity and school prayer; the uses of the word divide.

single-official-language.rationale: Roosevelt names a common language, the English language, first among the elemental things to secure, and the Americanization movement demanded quick acquisition and sole use of English.

social-market-economy.rationale: Rand's Textbook rejects any mixed system: a society that half-recognizes individual rights is disintegrating, not working.

socialized-markets.rationale: Read asks Americanists to oppose any socialistic activity, defined as state ownership and control of the means of production, and grounds America's growth in private property.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Roosevelt wants every man in the training camps to take the oath of allegiance as unreservedly as the regular army and navy.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Read calls Americanism's founding idea at once spiritual, political and economic and blames America's troubles on forgetting its spiritual antecedent.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Roosevelt's 1915 address wants the government to survey munition plants, plan new supply factories and conserve war materials, while Read condemns government invading the productive areas of society; the texts divide.

state-harmful.rationale: Rand's Textbook says the proper function of government is to protect individual rights and calls a state of anarchy savage, and the Legion preamble pledges to uphold the Constitution and maintain law and order.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Rand's Textbook says the collective cannot decide the purpose of a man's existence nor prescribe his choice of happiness.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Read praises the repeal of Britain's Corn Laws and the freedom of exchange preached by Cobden and Bright as the greatest reform in British history.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Thompson's definition says individuals should be able to dispose of their wealth without it being taken by the government, which a heavy tax on large inheritances does.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Thompson defines Americanism as holding that individuals may keep and dispose of their wealth without the government taking it, which a sharp rise in taxes on the rich contradicts.

taxation-theft.rationale: Read accepts taxes that pay for a government limited to inhibiting fraud and violence, recalling a take of 2 to 5 percent, and objects only to their growth.

total-state.rationale: Rand's Textbook says the power of society is limited by individual rights, and Thompson defines Americanism as separating church, school, economy and culture from the state.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Rand's Textbook gives Soviet Russia and Nazi Germany as the two examples of collectivism, and Read lists communism, fascism and Nazism as names of one disease.

traditional-family.rationale: Roosevelt calls the family the foundation stone of national life, but Thompson rejects the Right's identification of Americanism with family values as a European import opposed to its native meaning; the defining sources divide.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Roosevelt's 1915 address says Americans, though kin to every nation of Europe, are a new and distinct nationality.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Roosevelt demands that all citizens, Protestant and Catholic, Jew and Gentile, be treated exactly alike, with no discrimination for or against any creed.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Roosevelt wants nationwide government-paid training camps and universal military training for young men, which he says makes better citizens.

universal-morality.rationale: Rand's Textbook demands a defined, objective moral code and unalienable rights held by every man, and Thompson defends the Declaration's self-evident truths against the charge of imperialism.

workers-nation.rationale: Roosevelt wants every labour organisation subordinated to the service of the nation and calls those who follow the IWW enemies of the whole country.

workers-own-party.rationale: Roosevelt says no man who draws the political line between class and class is a good American, and the Legion pledges to combat the autocracy of classes.

missingStatements.text: Immigrants and citizens should owe political loyalty to one country alone, not divided between two.
missingStatements.rationale: Roosevelt rejected hyphenated Americanism and demanded loyalty acknowledging no flag but the American one.

missingStatements.text: One common language should be required of all citizens and used as the nation's language of public life.
missingStatements.rationale: Roosevelt named a common English language as a core requirement and treated refusal to learn it as refusing Americanization.

notes: Rules-5 pass by claude-opus-5-5 (2026-11-08), brought up to the shared rules because the page gets search traffic. The first pass (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-10-16) answered largely from Wikipedia's Americanism and American exceptionalism articles and from the Gettysburg Address, and recorded positions it judged adherents split on as 0. Under rules 5 Wikipedia is not evidence and the Gettysburg Address is not tied to Americanism by any defining source, so every first-pass answer was re-answered from the sources below or nulled, with the first version kept in its reviewHistory (s1, s4 and s5 stay listed for that history). This pass read in full Thompson's essay, the two Gale encyclopedia entries, Roosevelt's 1915 address and the 1894 excerpts, the Legion preamble and magazine account, Rand's Textbook (OCR of FEE's scan) and Read's speech. Themes searched: economy (property, welfare, taxes, trade, planning, inflation), government (democracy, Constitution, rights, majority rule), society and culture (religion, language, assimilation, race, education), liberty (force, self-ownership, censorship) and world (defence, conscription, loyalty, foreign influence). The defining sources say little on ecology, technology, alliances, the UN or social questions such as abortion and drugs, and Thompson's report that Left and Right attach opposite values to the word turns several society and economy statements into splits. Not read: Kazin and McCartin, Americanism: New Perspectives on the History of an Ideal (UNC Press 2006; no open copy, Everand preview only), Gelernter (2007), Wall (2008), the 1915 American Journal of Sociology symposium 'What is Americanism?' (a survey of 250 opinions, not a definition).
